study.title: Jeremiah 1 The call of the prophet and his commission before Judah
study.overview: Jeremiah 1 presents the beginning of Jeremiah's prophetic call as a direct conversation with the Lord. The chapter links the prophet's vocation to a concrete historical context, mentions his priestly origin in Anathoth and shows that his mission is born of God's sovereign initiative, not human preparation. The text emphasizes God's previous choice, the limitation recognized by Jeremiah himself, the promise of protection and two visions that announce imminent judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. In the end, the prophet is strengthened to resist the opposition, with the certainty that the presence of God will guarantee his perseverance.

outline.title: Registration and historical landmark of ministry
outline.explanation: The chapter opens identifying Jeremiah as the son of Hilkiah, the priest of Anathoth, and placing his activity in the days of Josiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, until the fall of Jerusalem. The text shows that its message develops over decades and amid the worsening of the national crisis.

outline.title: Called, objection and prophetic commission
outline.explanation: God reveals Jeremiah that he knew him and had separated him before birth. Jeremiah responds with a sense of incapacity to be young, but the Lord corrects him, promises to be with him, touches his mouth and puts his words in him, giving him a mission of judgment and also of reconstruction.

outline.title: Visions of the almond and boiling pot
outline.explanation: The two visions illustrate the speed of the fulfillment of the divine word and the arrival of invasion and terror through the north. The judgment is explained by the idolatry and the rupture of the covenant, for the people abandoned the Lord and worshipped works done by their own hands.

outline.title: End charge and promise of sustenance
outline.explanation: Jeremiah should prepare, stand up and speak without fear. God establishes him as a fortified city, a pillar of iron and bronze wall before leaders, priests and people; there will be a fight against him, but not the victory of the adversaries, because the Lord will be with him to deliver him.

study.context: The given notes place Jeremiah as the priest of Anathoth, a place associated with the priestly service in the land of Benjamin. The introduction of the book covers the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, ending with the deportation of Jerusalem. Tyndale notes that two brief kings do not appear on the list, which helps explain the historical sequence mentioned. Adam Clarke points out that Jeremiah's ministry began very young and extended for many years, until after the destruction of Jerusalem. The chapter therefore serves as the biographical and theological opening of the book, showing that the word of God comes to a prophet inserted in a real history of national decay.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the prophetic vocation is born from God's sovereign initiative: He knows, separates, calls and empowers even before the human response. The speech of God has real authority and concrete effect; when He says, His word does not fail or depend on the strength of the messenger. At the same time, the text preserves the responsibility of the prophet: Jeremiah must speak exactly what to receive, without fearing people. Theologically, the chapter unites judgment and restoration, because the same word that overthrows can also build and plant. The opposition is not denied; it is foreseen. Still, the presence of God is sufficient to sustain the faithful servant. The image of the touched mouth reinforces that the authority of the message comes from God, not from the natural eloquence of the prophet. The judgment announced against Judah is linked to the sin of forsake the Lord and practicing idolatry, showing that the unfaithfulness of the covenant brings real consequences.

scholarViews.insight: The call of Jeremiah is presented as a conversation in which God speaks with royal authority; the prophet's objections receive answers with decisive promises and visions.
Jeremiah is separated from the beginning to be a prophet to the nations, which shows that his submission does not depend on personal initiative, but on divine ordination.
Jeremiah, still very young, received the word from the Lord as an inspiration that gave him not only the subject, but also the words that he should pronounce.

questions: How is the certainty that God calls and sustains Jeremiah corrects our tendency to measure ministerial effectiveness only by human capacity?
In what ways does the chapter show that the word of God can both overthrow structures of sin and build what is in ruins?
What present day fears hinder clear obedience, and how the promise that the Lord delivers can confront them?
study.practice: Pray for God to align his mouth and heart to his word. Instead of expecting to feel fully ready, practice obedience to what has already been clearly revealed in the Scriptures. If you have to speak the truth in a hostile environment, remember that biblical courage is not an absence of opposition, but trust in the presence of God. Also examine whether there are subtle forms of idolatry, that is, to trust in what is done by human hands more than in the Lord. The chapter calls the believer to persevere without fear, with fidelity and clarity.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow to safely affirm all the biographical details of Jeremiah beyond what the chapter and commentators inform. The exact identification of Hilkiah in relation to other biblical characters remains only as a hypothesis in Matthew Henry's note, and not as a conclusive fact. The dating in years of the modern calendar appears only in Adam Clarke and was kept as observation of him, not as a certainty independent of the biblical text.
